Match peaks across chromatograms

Source: R/correct_rt.R
match_peaks.Rd

Matches peaks across chromatograms by spectral correlation and retention time proximity. Each reference peak is matched to at most one sample peak, taking candidate pairs in order of score, highest first. The resulting matched_peak_list object can be passed to correct_rt to perform landmark parametric time warping (alg = "lptw").

Usage

match_peaks(
  peak_list,
  chrom_list = NULL,
  reference = NULL,
  targets = NULL,
  lambda = NULL,
  rt_window = 0.3,
  spectral_cutoff = 0.95,
  background_correction = c("none", "linear"),
  rt_weight = 0.15,
  use_corrected_rt = NULL,
  spectral_test = c("cutoff", "noise"),
  alpha = 0.01,
  plot_it = FALSE,
  verbose = getOption("verbose")
)

Arguments

peak_list

A peak list object from get_peaks.

chrom_list

List of chromatograms in matrix format. If NULL, will be retrieved from the peak_list object.

reference

Index or name of the reference sample, or "best" to select the reference algorithmically using bestref. Defaults to NULL, which uses the first sample, or, if targets is given, a sample chosen from the targets.

targets

Optional table of targets, or a numeric vector of their retention times (see targeted_analysis). Used to choose the reference sample, unless reference is given, and to name the targets' columns in the peak table. See Targets and the reference sample. Cannot be combined with reference = "best". Defaults to NULL.

lambda

A character or numeric value specifying the wavelength to use for peak matching. Required if peaks were detected at multiple wavelengths, unless targets has a lambda column, which sets the wavelength per target; lambda then fills in targets without one.

rt_window

Numeric. Maximum allowed difference in retention time, in minutes, between a reference and sample peak to be considered a candidate match. An rt_window column in targets overrides it for those targets. Defaults to 0.3.

spectral_cutoff

Numeric. Minimum spectral correlation for a candidate peak pair to be retained. A spectral_cutoff column in targets overrides it for those targets. Ignored, with a warning, for one-dimensional chromatograms. Defaults to 0.95.

background_correction

How to correct the apex spectrum of each peak before correlating: "none" (the default) uses it as is, and "linear" subtracts the background under the peak, interpolated between the spectra at its start and end. See Background correction.

rt_weight

Numeric in [0, 1]. Penalizes retention time offset when ranking candidate pairs: each pair's spectral correlation is multiplied by 1 - rt_weight * d / rt_window, where d is the pair's retention time difference. At rt_weight = 1, a pair at the edge of the window scores zero. Defaults to 0.15.

use_corrected_rt

Logical. Whether to compare corrected retention times (rt.cor) from correct_peaks rather than raw ones (rt), both between peaks and against targets. Defaults to NULL, which uses corrected times when every sample has them.

spectral_test

How a candidate pair's spectra are compared: "cutoff" (the default) requires their correlation to be at least spectral_cutoff; "noise" tests whether they could be the same spectrum given each sample's noise, so that a small, noisy peak is not rejected for its noise alone. The "noise" test is experimental; see Testing spectra against noise.

alpha

Significance level for spectral_test = "noise". A pair is rejected if its p-value is below alpha. Pairs whose spectra are the same apart from noise are rejected at most about alpha of the time, except when the reference peak is small (up to roughly 20 times the noise), where they are rejected more often. Pairs whose spectra truly correlate at spectral_cutoff are rejected more often too, up to about half the time for peaks far above the noise, as with a correlation threshold. Defaults to 0.01.

plot_it

Logical. Whether to plot the matches with plot.matched_peak_list. Defaults to FALSE.

verbose

Whether to print messages to console.

Value

A matched_peak_list object: a list with one element per sample containing the matched peak pairs, per-pair spectral correlation scores, and peak data in index space for use with correct_rt. A sample with no peaks or no matches is NULL, with a warning. When targets is given, the targets with rt replaced by the reference's own retention times are stored as the "reference_targets" attribute. When the targets span several wavelengths, peaks are matched separately at each, and the result is a matched_peak_list_set: a list of matched_peak_list objects named by wavelength, which get_peaktable combines into one table. Unless reference is given, every wavelength uses the same reference sample, chosen from all the targets; if no sample contains every target, each wavelength gets its own, with a warning.

Targets and the reference sample

With targets, a sample's peak for a target is its tallest peak within tol of it that, when fitted, has r.squared of at least 0.5; a peak within tol of several targets counts only for the nearest. Unless reference is given, the reference is chosen among samples with a peak for every target, where a peak counts if it is at least a tenth of that target's median height across samples. The sample whose weakest target is largest relative to its median is chosen, then the one whose farthest peak lies closest to its target time.

Background correction

With background_correction = "linear", the apex spectrum is averaged over 2 scans either side and each boundary spectrum over 5 scans either side, to limit the noise the subtraction adds. The subtraction removes a background that varies linearly across the peak, such as a sloping baseline or a neighbor's tail. It also adds noise, and where a boundary lies on a neighboring peak it subtracts part of that peak's spectrum.

Testing spectra against noise

With spectral_test = "noise", each candidate pair is tested rather than thresholded. The sample spectrum is fitted as an offset plus a multiple of the reference spectrum by least squares, each wavelength weighted by the reciprocal of the sample's noise there. The hypothesis is that, without noise, the two spectra would correlate at spectral_cutoff; the residual that this mismatch would leave is subtracted, and what remains is compared with the residuals left under the same fit by pairs of noise spectra, one from the sample and one from the reference scaled by the fitted multiple. For a peak far above the noise, this reduces to requiring a noise-weighted correlation of at least spectral_cutoff; for a small peak, it allows for the noise, so a real peak is not rejected because its spectrum is noisy. Each matched sample's spectral_p holds the p-values of its matched pairs.

This test is experimental. It has had little testing on real data, and the way its p-values are calculated may change in future versions.

The noise spectra come from each chromatogram's own peak-free timepoints: those outside every peak in peak_list taller than 5 times its trace's noise, at any wavelength in peak_list, after dropping timepoints whose spectra still stand out from the rest. A trace's noise is the scaled median absolute deviation of its timepoints outside every peak taller than 3 times the noise, found by iterating from the estimate given by its point-to-point differences, mad(diff(y)) / sqrt(2) (von Neumann 1941; Donoho and Johnstone 1994).

The test cannot tell compounds apart near the noise level, where every spectrum is consistent with every other; decide whether a small peak is present by its height instead. A peak overlapped by a neighbor or sitting on structured background may be rejected because its apex spectrum really is a mixture. The test needs background_correction = "none" and, in each chromatogram, at least 30 peak-free timepoints and at least 1 / alpha, since with fewer it could never reject a match. On short traces with strongly autocorrelated noise, the peak-free timepoints are fewer independent spectra than their number, so a spectral_cutoff of 1 rejects identical spectra up to about twice as often as alpha.

References

  • Donoho, D. L., and Johnstone, I. M. 1994. Ideal spatial adaptation by wavelet shrinkage. Biometrika 81:425-455. doi:10.1093/biomet/81.3.425 .

  • von Neumann, J. 1941. Distribution of the ratio of the mean square successive difference to the variance. Ann. Math. Stat. 12:367-395. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177731677 .

Examples

data(Sa_pr)
pks <- get_peaks(Sa_pr, lambdas = 210, fit = "egh")
match_peaks(pks, lambda = 210)
#> A matched_peak_list with 4 samples, matched at 210 nm against reference sample 119
#> Reference peaks: 29 | spectral_cutoff: 0.95 | background correction: none
#> Matched peaks per sample: 121 12, 122 18, 458 17
